rows.e: EO 13848 (foreign-election-interference emergency) sets the post-election channel: sec. 1(a) DNI assessment "Not later than 45 days after the conclusion of" the election, to the President and the Secretaries of State, Treasury, Defense, the AG and DHS; sec. 1(b) AG and DHS report "Within 45 days of receiving" that assessment, to the President and Secretaries of State, Treasury and Defense, on whether foreign interference "materially affected the security or integrity" of election infrastructure, tabulation or transmission of results; sec. 1(c) all agencies send relevant information to the DNI and reports are amended on new information; sec. 2 Treasury blocking sanctions; sec. 3 review and sanctions after the reports. "Election infrastructure" includes "voter registration databases" (sec. 8(d)); "foreign interference" includes acts with the purpose or effect of "undermining public confidence in election processes" (sec. 8(f)). For Nov 3, 2026: 1(a) due by Dec 18, 2026; 1(b) due within 45 days after 1(a) is received, about Feb 1, 2027 if 1(a) comes Dec 18; both can come earlier.
rows.w: The emergency later renewed each year (Aug 31, 2026); its post-election assessment is the formal foreign-interference finding vehicle
rows.s: EO 13848, 83 FR 46843 (Sept 14, 2018), FR Doc. 2018-20203, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2018/09/14/2018-20203/imposing-certain-sanctions-in-the-event-of-foreign-interference-in-a-united-states-election, secs. 1-3, 8(d), 8(f) (fetched Oct 28, 2026) · EO 13848 (UCSB Presidency Project) · EO 13848 (presidency.ucsb.edu) · EO 13848, Federal Register

rows.e: Cyber Response and Recovery Act (P.L. 117-58 div. G sec. 70602, enacted Nov 15, 2021; 6 U.S.C. 677-677g): the DHS Secretary, "in consultation with the National Cyber Director," may declare a "significant incident" (an incident or group of related incidents that results, or "is likely to result," in demonstrable harm to national security, foreign relations or the economy, or to "the public confidence, civil liberties, or public health and safety" (677a(8)); national security systems excluded) that has occurred or "is likely to occur imminently" where other resources "are likely insufficient" (677b(a)(1)); the Secretary "may not delegate" the power (677b(a)(2)). Upon a declaration the CISA Director "shall coordinate" the asset response activities of each federal agency, and "shall coordinate" with federal, state, local and Tribal law enforcement "with respect to investigations and threat response activities" (677b(b)(2)(B)). The declaration must be published in the Federal Register within 72 hours (no names of affected people or companies) (677b(e)); the Secretary may act in advance, including "entering into standby contracts with private entities for cybersecurity services" (677b(f)); the National Cyber Director and congressional committees are notified "immediately," and the notice must name "if known, the perpetrator of the specific significant incident" (677d(a)(2)(B)); a declaration lasts 120 days or less, renewable by the Secretary; the Cyber Response and Recovery Fund can make grants for "hardware or software to replace, update, improve, harden" ($20M/yr FY2022-FY2028); assistance to non-federal entities is "voluntary"; authorities expire Nov 15, 2028; never publicly used. A Paperwork Reduction Act waiver for voluntary collection, claimed in earlier notes, was not found in the 677-677g text fetched Oct 28 (U).
rows.s: 6 U.S.C. 677, 677a(8), 677b(a)-(f), 677c(a), 677d, 677f, 677g (govinfo USCODE-2023 / LII, fetched Oct 28, 2026); P.L. 117-58 div. G sec. 70602 · https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/6/677a ; /677b ; /677d (fetched Oct 28, 2026, item 3 check)

rows.e: SBA and DHS/FEMA computer matching agreement to re-establish the disaster-aid duplication match (prior match set to expire Aug 21, 2025; file dated May 28, 2025, signature date lines blank in the text). FEMA's ORR Recovery Reporting and Analytics Division sends SBA an encrypted cumulative registrant file by SFTP at least once per business day (all disasters declared on or after Mar 22, 2024), including every household occupant's name, age, SSN and relationship, pre-disaster gross income, number of dependents, special-needs flag, vehicles, insurance policies and flood data; SBA returns verified losses, loan approvals, disbursements and decline codes and pushes loan status back; SBA queries FEMA in real time (SOAP/XML web service over HTTPS); 18 months plus one 12-month renewal; effective 30 days after FR notice or 40 days after the report to OMB and Congress, whichever is later.
rows.w: Baseline of a lawful Privacy Act (o) match with DIB, notice and congressional report; no citizenship, immigration or voter fields. Sec. XV lets both OIGs use match results "for investigation, audit, or evaluation"; sec. XII sends FEMA and SBA online applicants' name, address, SSN and DOB to an unnamed "commercial database provider" for identity verification; sec. VI bars adverse action before written notice and a chance to contest (5 USC 552a(p)). This is the due-process template the DOJ/DHS voter-roll transfers did not follow (I; benign reading: the government says those transfers rest on other authorities that need no CMA).

rows.e: 2024 EAVS: 1,736,209 provisional ballots (0.9% of voters), 73.8% counted, 25.1% rejected; most common reason cast: voter "did not appear on the list of eligible voters" (40.2%); most common reason rejected: not registered in the state (52.2%). Mail: 66.9M sent, 47.96M returned, 584,463 rejected (1.2%; 40.7% signature), 585,457 entered cure, over half cured; UOCAVA 1.3M+ sent, 806,743 returned, under 4% rejected; 7,795 FWABs not counted.
rows.w: Provisional ballots are the existing mechanism through which a "hold" works: a voter flagged or dropped from the list votes provisionally, and one in four provisional ballots is rejected nationally; mail and UOCAVA ballots already pass signature and deadline screens an added citizenship hold would stack on (I). Benign: ordinary baseline statistics.

rows.e: DHS posts the RAVEn PIA-055 appendix update (dhs.gov 25_0618 file; reprints the May 13, 2020 base PIA plus current appendices): RAVEn ingests FinCEN BSA reports daily ("subject biographic information, bank account information, occupation, passport number, country, amount and type of transactions"); SSA sends yearly the earnings reported on SSNs "assigned to non-immigrants who are not authorized to be employed" (8 USC 1360(c)(2); SSN, name, address, employer name and address, earnings, tax year; purged after processing unless marked pertinent); PRAC PPP/EIDL loan data with nationality; ARC TIP airline data daily (previous day's ticket sales, 39 months of past and future travel, over 1 billion records, searchable by passenger name, credit card number, airport code and ticketing dates; ICE's derived queries kept 45 days); HORUS face images temporary by default, only unidentified images in an HSI program gallery kept 75 years; RAVEn GO alerts; OBIM IDENT/HART on-demand queries; Lead Tracking Tool rejection reasons only resources, prosecutor declined and "Other" (no "inaccurate match/likely citizen"); App. A lists no USCIS system, SAVE, voter file, IRS, Do Not Pay or Treasury tip source despite saying it "will be updated" when new data is ingested. App. A refresh cadence: ICM, EID, DTS (detainee calls), Pen-Link, BMIS, EARS, SEN, the ICE Subpoena System and FinCEN BSA daily; NCIC and IDENT/HART on demand; TRAC (state-run money-services-business database) on demand under an MOU; USDA NFC payroll ad hoc.
rows.w: Passport-number match key in HSI analytics. The PIA omits the voter rolls HSI iLab processes: either that processing sits outside RAVEn or the PIA was not updated (E-Government Act gap). CORE's "Individuals Impacted" covers people in "U.S. passport, visa, border, immigration, and naturalization benefit data" via the DHS/ICE-018 SORN pool, so the PIA scope does not exclude USCIS/State data; it just names no source entry for them (I).
rows.sy: ICE-05 RAVEn, RAVEn GO, Lead Tracking Tool, HORUS; FinCEN BSA; SSA MEF; PRAC; ARC TIP; OBIM IDENT/HART

rows.e: DHS/USCIS final rule on USCIS law-enforcement authorities (90 FR 42797, FR Doc. 2025-16978; published Sept 5, effective Oct 6, 2025) codifies arrest, warrant and firearms authority for officers the Director designates and lets designated supervisory officials initiate criminal investigations (Delegation 15006; 8 CFR 287.2); describes FDNS as the information-sharing conduit; ICE keeps "sole responsibility" for criminal benefit-fraud investigations; MOAs "will be updated"; "DHS is not recombining USCIS and ICE." The rule does not itself say FDNS is designated law enforcement (FDNS appears only in the background section). Issued without notice and comment under the 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A) "procedural" exception as "internal house-keeping"; DHS says it is not a CRA "rule" (5 U.S.C. 804(3)(C)) but sent it to Congress and GAO; claims no federalism implications; signed by Secretary Kristi Noem; filed Sept 4, 2025. The Director may designate individuals "or a class of individuals" to make warrantless arrests for offenses in the officer's presence and for felonies (287.5(c)), execute search warrants and serve arrest warrants (287.5(e)), carry firearms (287.5(f)(8)), and use non-deadly and deadly force and vehicular pursuit (287.8); sets "substantially equivalent" training (287.1(g)); and must issue search-and-seizure and firearms guidelines (287.9).
rows.w: USCIS turned partly law-enforcement. Who decides: the USCIS Director designates who becomes an armed, arresting officer; no outside check is written into the rule.
rows.s: DHS/USCIS final rule, USCIS law-enforcement authorities, 90 FR 42797, FR Doc. 2025-16978 (published Sept 5, 2025; effective Oct 6, 2025) · FR 2025-16978

rows.e: DHS publishes modified SORN DHS/USCIS-004 SAVE (90 FR 48948-48955, FR Doc. 2025-19735, docket USCIS-2025-0337): adds U.S. citizens by birth; adds full/truncated SSN, U.S. passport number, driver's-license number and SSA-supplied data; adds record sources SSA-60-0058 (Numident), State STATE-05/-26/-39 and driver's-license agencies such as NLETS (DL search "not live at the time of publication"); clarifies voter verification and says it is "reinserting voter registration that was previously published in 76 FR 58525" as an administrative clarification; SSN case creation and the list processor were limited at first to web-browser users, and the list processor creates individual cases ("this is not batch processing"); a new oversight account type may view other user agencies' case data linked "by benefit type ... or by state"; new routine uses L (SSA and other authorized entities) and M (oversight/auditing) effective Dec 1, 2025; keeps routine use G (disclosure to law-enforcement agencies investigating violations of law) while stating SAVE information "is not to be used for administrative (non-criminal) immigration enforcement purposes." Prior version 85 FR 31798 (May 27, 2020); comments due Dec 1, 2025 (the SORN gives no comment count; the "9,361" in earlier notes needs a docket cite, U); exemptions "None." SSA published its companion Numident SORN modification Nov 12, 2025 (90 FR 50879; effective Dec 12, 2025).
rows.w: SAVE overhauled for voter checks and formally covers U.S.-born citizens; criminal referral stays permitted on the SORN face (routine use G).
rows.s: DHS/USCIS-004 SAVE SORN, 90 FR 48948-48955, FR Doc. 2025-19735, Oct 31, 2025, docket USCIS-2025-0337, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-10-31/html/2025-19735.htm (Summary, Supplementary Information, routine uses A, G, I, L, M, DATES)

rows.e: SAVE PIA DHS/USCIS/PIA-006(d) (Oct 31, 2025) documents five changes: voter-registration and voter-list-maintenance verification; collection of SSNs "which may include those of U.S. born citizens"; sharing among USCIS, SSA and States; a bulk "list processor"; no fee for non-federal agencies. SAVE queries 20 federal systems: USCIS (CIS, ELIS, CLAIMS 3, eCISCOR, GLOBAL, RAILS, Customer Profile Management System, Salesforce CRM), other DHS (OneNet, ICE SEVP, ICE EID, CBP ADIS, TSA OIA TIM) and other federal (MEPCOM, IRS, ED FSA CPS, HHS CMS, SSA Numident, DOJ EOIR IRIES, State CCD, State ACRQ). SAVE "will maintain and process" State-submitted data on U.S.-born citizens and keeps case records 10 years from verification (NARA N1-566-08-07) or until an ongoing law-enforcement investigation ends. SAVE verifies U.S. passport numbers against State records and "will receive or access" State's CCD / American Citizen Record Query (USCIS sends State name, DOB, SSN and/or passport number); uses driver's-license/state ID numbers to validate identity and "gain access to other government enumerators" through state DMVs or NLETS; adds an oversight account type through which user agencies "with legal authority" may view other agencies' SAVE case data by benefit type or "by state" and re-check people already granted benefits (SORN routine use M). The PIA concedes SSN-based queries cannot get SAVE's second (manual) or third (documents) verification step because USCIS "does not have direct access" to the SSA system, rates the inaccurate-information risk only "partially" mitigated, and notes agencies "may not go through all steps"; "When potential fraud or misuse is indicated," information may be shared case by case with ICE and CBP.
rows.w: SAVE is a lookup service, so orders against "SAVE" may not reach the underlying data; but SAVE itself keeps every submitted voter record and the SSA/State responses 10+ years. Version change: PIA-006(c) (Jun 30, 2020) said SAVE data "will not be used for administrative (non-criminal) immigration enforcement purposes"; 006(d) drops that line and lists ICE and CBP as case-by-case recipients when fraud or misuse is indicated.

rows.e: On or around May 8, 2026, USCIS FDNS receives the California voter roll from HSI for noncitizen review (the roll was purchased from the California Secretary of State, buyer not named, and given to HSI by a DHS senior counselor about Mar 19; it holds name, address and DOB, no SSN or ID numbers); FDNS then enhances it with Accurint data. FDNS Associate Director Bartell says USCIS "receives state voter rolls or information on state voter rolls from DHS," analyzes them and refers matches to HSI. HSI's Eric McLoughlin says HSI "initially reviewed the list of millions of registered voters in California" and "formatted and delivered" it without changing data, and describes HSI's statewide role as "data intake (including obtaining bona fide voter rolls), preparation, enrichment, quality review, and routing of leads" (Dkt. 62-3 paras 11, 14, 20). The roll reflects voter registration as of Aug 2025.
rows.w: Documents the HSI-to-FDNS hand-off and commercial enrichment of a state roll; SoS release-letter limits on onward transfer bear on it (I). About a seven-week HSI hold (Mar 19 to about May 8) before FDNS; HSI is the intake hub for state rolls; the list DOJ sent Oct 13 was built from a roll dated Aug 2025, about seven months old when HSI received it (I).

rows.e: DHS-CISA guide (DHS and CISA seals on the cover) "Recognizing and Addressing Threats to Statewide Voter Registration Databases" (cover date July 2026; 11 pp.; no named author) opens: "Recently declassified records revealed that China breached multiple state voter registration systems prior to the 2020 election" (no footnote) and "Hackers have attempted to breach voter registration systems in all 50 states, with confirmed successes in at least 20 states" (no footnote); it says "experts have routinely minimized" breaches, that this "makes U.S. elections less secure," and that candor reduces "vulnerability to worst case scenarios." Its own breach history (pp.2-3) lists no Chinese breach of a state voter registration system: the PRC entries are 2021 critical-infrastructure targeting (fn 10, Jul 19, 2021 NSA/CISA/FBI advisory) and 2022 suspected PRC actors who "scanned" state websites and "collected publicly available U.S. voter information" (fn 13, the DOJ/DHS 2022 Key Findings, which also found no compromise of voter-registration integrity); the other entries are Russia 2016, Illinois and Arizona 2016, Riverside County 2016 (domestic), Kennesaw State 2017 (exposure), Iran IRGC 2020 (one state), pro-Russian DDoS 2022 and a 2023 New Hampshire offshoring issue; nothing listed adds up to 20 states. its source is U (possibly the Jul 30 White House fact sheet/, or another version). First public release: in the White House declassification trove on Jul 16, 2026 (zip "4. Noncitizens on State Voter Rolls"); cisa.gov posting later (2026-09 folder).
rows.w: D that CISA said it; the truth of the China-breach claim is U and is contradicted by the guide's own list and its own fn 13 source (D vs D). Concern step 1: the foreign-hack predicate written into a federal product addressed to the officials who run the rolls; it discredits caution in advance ("minimized") and closes with "collaborate with DHS" (I). Benign reading: a threat-awareness guide summarizing the July declassification. The copy in the White House trove has CreationDate Jun 24, 2026 and ModDate Jul 13, 2026 17:55 EDT, and its text is identical to the Sept 16 cisa.gov copy (text diff empty), so the "China breached" sentence was in the final file by Jul 13: after the Jul 3/Jul 10 declassification marks, the same day as the Task Force "compromised" statement and three days before the public release (D, metadata). "CISA" alone understates DHS: the guide carries both seals. Posting: see the Sept 24 row. ODNI timing: the declassification marks on the trove name President Trump (Jul 3), Counsel to the President Warrington (Jul 10), DNI Gabbard (Mar 16, one memo) and D/CIA Ratcliffe (Jul 1, one note); none names acting DNI Pulte (in office about Jul 1-Aug 3). The guide was finalized Jul 13, before Clayton became DNI (Aug 3).

It asks states to keep frequent offline backups and test reverting, print paper pollbook backups, run incident-response and continuity plans on unauthorized access, and follow cyber basics (MFA, DMARC, DDoS arrangements, KEV patching within 15 days, segmentation, EDR, .gov, MDBR, 30-day encrypted offline backups); it treats CISA Binding Operational Directives as best practice "While not binding on non-Federal entities" and ends: state officials "are encouraged to collaborate with DHS."
rows.w: A federal rationale for treating state rolls as possibly corrupted, the predicate a later "verify your rolls against federal data" demand would cite (I). Benign: standard resilience guidance; the remedies are state-run, and paper pollbooks are a safeguard against a "nobody votes until feds validate" scenario. The guide claims no power to require anything (BODs "not binding").

It cites 2026 HUD SORN amendments: IMS/PIC (HUD/PIH.01, 91 FR 2137, Jan 16 and 91 FR 22845, Apr 28), TRACS (HUD/HOU-11, 91 FR 22160, Apr 24) and EIV (HUD/PIH-05, 91 FR 34245, Jun 5), whose routine uses (EIV RU 4, TRACS RU 13 as the CMA paraphrases them) allow disclosure to federal agencies, non-federal entities and contractors "for preventing, detecting, and investigating fraud, waste, and abuse." Match processes: a sheltering/housing match first on name, address, DOB and last-4 SSN and then full fields, and FEMA sends HUD every IA registration per disaster (including gross income).
rows.w: Fraud/duplication matching; the "fraud, waste, and abuse" routine-use wording is the phrase trail. Whether the 2026 HUD SORN changes tie to HUD citizenship or mixed-status verification is I/U (SORN texts not read). Sec. VI "records relating to U.S. citizens" is standard protection text, not a citizenship check.

rows.a: House Oversight Subcommittee on Government Operations
rows.e: House Oversight Subcommittee on Government Operations holds "Emerging Fraud Threats and the Evolving Fraud Landscape" (Serial No. 119-70; Sessions chair; 2:03-3:58 p.m.; most majority members absent for an Administration Middle East briefing). Witnesses: Jordan Burris (Socure Vice President and Head of Public Sector Strategy; former Chief of Staff, White House Office of the Federal CIO), Marisol Cruz Cain (GAO IT & Cybersecurity), David Maimon (SentiLink, Georgia State) and Jay Stanley (ACLU, minority witness). Burris says "identity should be considered critical infrastructure" and that Socure is a Login.gov vendor after competing against 17 others (document verification, facial biometric comparison, device and fraud models); a citation of DHS/CISA naming identity management a National Critical Function is in our notes from his written statement but is not in the printed record (U). Sessions proposes that Login.gov identity-verification failures (who failed, where, how) be studied and moved "to the organization we talked about this morning, to Pandemic Response Accountability Committee (PRAC)," says Congress will make PRAC's data effort permanent, and asks whether it is "fair game to go back and run people back through" benefit programs because "a lot of people that presently are receiving government benefits might not be exactly as we thought they were," and whether AI flags (e.g., "74 people at your home address") can trigger review. Rep. Randall enters the Wired article "A DOGE Affiliate Is Now in Charge of the US Government ID Platform"; Ranking Member Mfume says DOGE used an SSA identity database to mark people. GAO: Login.gov meets NIST IAL2 after a remote identity-proofing pilot, agencies lack visibility into why users fail, 100M+ users, 50+ agencies, 500 applications incl. state and local. Industry witnesses (SentiLink, Socure) urge "real-time cross-agency data matching," holding payments via an expanded Do Not Pay, continuous identity re-verification and "historical signals" from commercial data.

rows.e: In a primetime address Trump says he is declassifying documents on China's alleged acquisition of U.S. voter records, calling it "the largest compromise of election data in history" (the Jul 30 White House fact sheet later says up to 220 million records; coverage of the address cites "about 200 million" in some intelligence reporting); he says a DHS review found ~278,000 noncitizens registered and that the "deep state" hid it. BBC reports Trump said 18 states' voter data was taken by China (BBC's exact words and how they relate to the Jul 30 Task Force fact sheet: see), and he says that "My administration is in the process of notifying the states whose election data was compromised by the People's Republic of China and many others," and that he will help states "fix and patch known technical vulnerabilities before the midterm elections"; "I've also ordered DHS to notify every state about noncitizens on their voter rolls and direct them to remove all ineligible voters from the lists immediately." Earlier that evening a White House official previewed "five main revelations," said 220 million files were "compromised" by China between 2020 and 2023, and said the material did not allege that votes were changed or machines hacked; the release ran to "hundreds of pages," many heavily redacted (BBC). David Becker (CEIR) on the 278,000 figure: based on commercial data, "a ton of false positives" (CBS fact check 10:45 PM). Mullin: "We know that they can change voter registration and your vote" (limiting record released by the same White House, D: the 2020 Election Day log records one real unauthorized voter-address change in a Florida county through a known state website flaw that FBI/CISA were already working, no foreign attribution, and "no significant nefarious Chinese election-related activities," Election Day Log pp.14, 25-30, 69); the declassified release includes a CISA review of vulnerabilities in election IT networks; the documents show no altered votes, and officials in 12 of 15 named states say they were never notified (R). Counterpoint (D): no released document read gives 220 million or a 2020-2023 range; the largest voter figure is 204,822,241 records of "Unspecified U.S. voter data" dated 2016 on a list a PRC actor possessed "as of [redacted] 2019" (200M Voter Records p.3, B13).
rows.w: China voter-roll "breach" predicate (step 1 of the sequence).

rows.e: DHS sends "preliminary review" letters to states that refused DOJ: California 190,832 flagged, Nevada 15,903, Pennsylvania 14,576. Nevada later says all 185 voters DHS "confirmed" were citizens; for Pennsylvania DHS "did not have high confidence." Trump claims "approximately 278,000 non-citizens" The complaint says only part of each list matched on full name, DOB, address and SSN: California 81,336 of 190,832; Nevada 8,576 of 15,903; Pennsylvania 8,594 of 14,576; how the rest were flagged is not explained (R, DSCC complaint paras 60, 64, 69). DHS's own sheet ("Preventing Alien Voting," data as of Jun 22) says its 250,000 came from "public voter files from states that have not utilized the SAVE system" (CA, PA, NJ, NV); the White House Jul 17 page restates it as ~278,000 in four states "that cooperated with the Department's request," which contradicts DHS's description (D vs D). Nevada: DHS initially identified up to 15,903 on "high-confidence" matches, "later reduced that number to 6,218, and then to 185 after conducting its manual review"; Nevada confirmed all 185 were citizens; Judge Carter relies on this sequence in finding DOJ's process not credible (ECF 149 p.22, citing NAACP Opp. Dkt 37-1 at 20; underlying numbers from the NAACP brief, NPR, NYT).

rows.a: White House Government Transparency Task Force
rows.e: White House Government Transparency Task Force Fact Sheet (Jul 30, 2026; original not on disk; listed by title and date in the "Related" box of the Jul 17 "Setting the Record Straight" page) says, as quoted in reporting, that China and its proxies "bought, stole, or hacked as many as 220 million Americans' voter registration data," including "non-publicly available data"; that the directors of ODNI, NSA, CIA and DHS "approved the factual statements" used in the Jul 16 speech; and that declassified 2022 IC documents describe a Chinese computer-network-exploitation actor that acquired voter data "stored on commercial websites" (IANS, Jul 31). Reporting also attributes to it the IC definition that targeting voter-registration infrastructure or data is election interference, and a claim that possession could let an adversary alter registrations or force voters into provisional ballots (R). BBC attributes similar wording ("bought, stolen or hacked by China," of 18 states' data) to the Jul 16 speech itself (BBC, Jul 17; R). FactCheck.org calls "compromised" misleading; coverage adds tens of millions of files from 18 states in 2020, 220 million by 2023, purchased vs stolen not determined; WaPo: 12 of 15 named states were never notified; CISA is discussing victim notifications (R). rows.e: Census Bureau posts (Aug 18, 2026; dated "AUGUST 2026") an unauthored brief, "Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election, A Beginning Analysis" (approval CBDRB-FY26-0285): "over 24,000" noncitizen voter records in 2020 with "over 32 million" records still to analyze. Every federal record reaches a voter only through a match to the DataClear 2020 commercial voter file, linked by PVS to PIKs built from SSA Numident; sources are USCIS green-card/LPR records, State immigrant and nonimmigrant visas, ICE records ("foreign students, removals, and national-docket proceedings"), USCIS DACA approvals, SSA legal-alien citizenship codes and IRS ITINs ("an affirmative noncitizen signal"); ~63,800 voters naturalized before 2020 are cleared and ~7,000 of the 24,000 have no country of birth. It cites the Bureau's "crime" statistics authority and reports no false-positive rate (it cites a 2014 PVS false-match paper without applying it). NPR reports non-career staff with America First Policy Institute ties did the work; Trump says the number will "explode" (R). Title 13 bars sharing the names. Method (App. 1-2): voters are cleared on SSA citizen codes and U.S. birth (82.7% of confirmed citizens), passports and naturalization oaths; anyone found in any federal noncitizen source (including ITIN holders, DACA recipients and foreign students) is presumed a noncitizen "unless citizenship evidence establishes" otherwise; the DataClear file was bought in 2024 for undercount research.
rows.w: Federal statistical "2020 foundation" for noncitizen-voting claims, built on repurposed administrative data.
rows.sy: Census admin records; NUMIDENT; PVS; Census; DataClear; FDNS/USC-06

rows.e: DHS Secretary Mullin writes Attorney General Blanche (Sept 2, 2026, on its face; scanned on whitehouse.gov as AG-Letter-S1-Signed.pdf), congratulating him on his confirmation "earlier this month" and, invoking DHS's Sector Risk Management Agency role for election infrastructure, informing him of "prior referrals" DHS made to DOJ "during my predecessor's tenure" (Noem); it makes no new requests and asks DOJ to "review these referrals." Referral 1: whether voting systems that count from barcodes or QR codes comply with HAVA Title III's voter-verifiable paper record and manual-audit requirement, 52 U.S.C. 21081(a)(2)(B); it cites EO 14248 and the CISA report in the White House "Vulnerabilities-in-Electronic-Voting-and-Ballot-Counting-Systems.zip" (p.4: hackers "could change the votes encoded in the barcode"). Referral 2: legality under the DPPA (18 U.S.C. 2721-2725) of states sharing motor-vehicle and voter data with ERIC and, via ERIC, with CEIR; DHS and DOJ met on it in Sept 2025. The letter asserts the ERIC model contract requires MVA data every 60 days and bars sending records indicating non-citizenship; cites a 2022 Colorado mailer to ~30,000 noncitizens, a 2026 Georgia SAVE run finding >42,000 deceased registrants, and a Feb 2026 Renton, WA ballots-by-dumpster claim (sourced to the Skagit County GOP); quotes the ERIC founder on Democratic targeting; and closes "as we support the President's America First agenda." It does not mention recounts and does not ask DOJ to investigate whether election nonprofits "improperly obtained" data in those words (earlier NOTUS/NYT summaries, R).
rows.w: A DHS (SRMA) -> DOJ enforcement referral channel against machines (branch C) and a multistate list-maintenance nonprofit and civic grantmaker (branch B), opened under Noem and re-pushed to Blanche two months before the election. rows.e: FBI story (Sept 17, 2026): the DOJ National Fraud Detection Center (NFDC), "Launched in August" under DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division (Acting AAG Colin McDonald) and stemming from the "whole of government" approach "mandated by Executive Order 14395," "combines cross-agency data and artificial intelligence" and "utilizes an advanced AI environment to comb through vast data troves"; inaugural partners are the FBI, HSI, IRS-CI, FinCEN, PRAC, the Treasury Department and "numerous federal Inspectors General," and the center "also includes officials from multiple states"; the FBI "contributes Bureau data while gaining access to information shared by partner agencies"; a Division Fraud Counsel in every U.S. Attorney's Office receives "streamlined investigative packages—like pre-drafted search warrant affidavits and complaint language—to target multi-jurisdictional networks"; in a student-loan case the FBI opened "over 40 cases across 27 different field offices" tied to "the same group of actors overseas" (section chief Kevin Gallagher); a "Most Wanted Fraudsters" list launched in June.
rows.w: Template package pipeline from fused data to warrants and complaints, written centrally and sent to every U.S. Attorney's Office: the affidavit a magistrate judge sees can be drafted by the national center (I). The "actors overseas" framing turns local cases into one foreign-directed, multi-district scheme (compare Rule 41(b)(6), any-district warrants, I). Benign: program-fraud enforcement (Medicaid, Medicare, FAFSA, SBA).

rows.e: Bartell declaration (CNA v. Mullin ECF 46-1): USCIS compares voter information from states, public and "other lawfully available data ... against DHS and commercial database holdings" (¶10); before the LWV order SAVE referred positive non-citizen matches to FDNS, and "Following the LWV order, SAVE stopped referring such information to FDNS," but FDNS kept using what SAVE had referred because it was by then held under the FDNS SORN (¶¶12-13); SAVE referrals were "only a small portion" of what FDNS reviewed (¶14); FDNS weighed "the possibility that in rare circumstances U.S. citizens might be incorrectly identified as aliens" and proceeded (¶17). Bartell says EO 14248 prompted FDNS to review noncitizens and naturalized citizens who may have voted before naturalization (para 9) and that FDNS "is not a SAVE User Agency" (n.1; para 15); FDNS's new Criminal Investigative Division is "not directly involved in the investigations into unlawful voting" (para 7); FDNS closes a review on derived/acquired citizenship or discrepancies except where data suggest voting or registration before naturalization (para 19). Our Draft 1.2 notes also cite the declarations for SAVE being a point-in-time query service (paragraph not confirmed).
rows.w: FDNS keeps working outside SAVE while SAVE is blocked; court orders on SAVE do not reach copies already held under another SORN. Sworn admission that citizen voters can be misidentified by a law-enforcement unit matching against commercial data outside SAVE (para 17).

rows.a: DOJ (United States v. Alaska, D. Alaska 3:26-cv-00376-SLG)
rows.e: DOJ sues in United States v. Alaska (D. Alaska 3:26-cv-00376-SLG) to bar certification of the Senate race if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, defining "voter confusion" as a loss where votes for a second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, would have made him win under ranked-choice voting; it calls this "consistent with the NVRA"; its single count rests on "NVRA, 52 U.S.C. §§ 20501(b)(3), 20510(a)" (the purposes clause and the AG enforcement provision), plus Bullock v. Carter and Jenness v. Fortson (ECF 1); ¶44 asks that certification be barred "pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan"; it relies on Director Beecher's June 15, 2026 finding of a candidacy filed "to confuse or mislead." Defendants are the State of Alaska, Director Carol Beecher, the Election Boards and the State Ballot Counting Review Board; a "Final Determination Letter" is attached to the complaint. Filing: "it is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion." Trump, Oct 23: "Well, I'm one that said, 'Do it.'" The complaint is signed Oct 22 by Associate AG Stanley E. Woodward Jr. and AUSA E. Bryan Wilson; a federal grand jury had earlier been convened on the second Dan Sullivan (R). Jen Psaki called the suit a "pretext" (Oct 24, R, Raw Story).
rows.w: Federal action against certification at the President's direction ("Do it"); the "integrity of the electoral process" phrase joins the phrase trail.

rows.a: USCIS FDNS Assoc. Dir. Nicolas Bartell / DOJ
rows.e: Bartell Declaration #2 (US v. California ECF 107-2, executed and filed Oct 26 for the Oct 27 TRO hearing before Judge Carter) lays out the FDNS pipeline: roll "purchased from the California Secretary of State and provided to HSI" (Ex. A; buyer not named; no SSNs), reaching HSI about Mar 19 from "a DHS senior counselor" (107-3 ¶5) and FDNS about May 8 (¶21); six fields sent to LexisNexis Accurint, which returns aliases, SSNs, DOBs, dates of death, phones and addresses (¶15); paired with A-numbers (¶16); name+DOB+SSN queries to State and SSA, none without an SSN (¶17); FDNS confidence levels (¶18) and two-level manual review (¶19); refined list to HSI (¶22), which "continued to further refine the data with federal law enforcement systems" (62-3 ¶23); 20,930 names delivered to California Oct 13, ~189 with "minor data discrepancies" (n.1); 17,000+ more under review, "most ... will end up being referred to HSI" (¶24). Bartell: FDNS Associate Director since July 2026, senior counselor to the USCIS Director Sept 2025-Jul 2026, Acting AD Apr-Jul 2026. USCIS receives records "on a rolling basis before the election date" (para 24). A companion Bartell declaration on LA County's 200-name sample (Dkt 107-1, same day) says USCIS found 51 people on the DHS list whose California roll entry gives a U.S. birthplace, but that none matched to the sample were U.S.-born per USCIS records; re-review found 4 who "might have a claim to U.S. citizenship" and 1 deceased (paras 6-13, n.1, Ex. C).
rows.w: Government's own sworn account of the outside-SAVE identity pipeline. The SSN that drives the State/SSA citizen screen comes from Accurint, not the roll - a wrong commercial SSN can make the screen miss a citizen (I; benign reading: multi-field match plus manual review is meant to catch that).

rows.a: Judge David O. Carter, C.D. Cal. (United States v. California, No. 2:26-cv-12025)
rows.e: Judge Carter DENIES DOJ's TRO application (Dkt 62) to make California and Los Angeles County segregate and not count the vote-by-mail ballots of ~20,000 people on the "October List" (ECF 149, 26 pp.). Holdings at the likelihood-of-success stage, not final merits: (1) the U.S. likely lacks Article III standing no "interference" with 18 U.S.C. 611 enforcement (DOJ is actively charging people; refusing to help is not impeding, US v. California, 921 F.3d 865), it cannot "spend its way into standing," and vote dilution is too speculative (Clapper, Lake v. Fontes); (2) no cause of action the Supremacy Clause creates none (Armstrong) and there is no equitable tradition of commandeering state election officials; (3) Section 611 does not preempt California election law no conflict, the Elections Clause leaves procedure to the states absent a clear congressional statement (Gregory v. Ashcroft; ITCA), and the theory raises Tenth Amendment anti-commandeering problems; (4) the relief would likely violate the NVRA 90-day bar (the October List is a "systematic" program like the data-match in Mi Familia Vota v. Fontes; "temporary segregation" has the same effect as removal: "a ballot segregated, in effect, would be a ballot removed," because neither DOJ which admits it cannot verify before Election Day, Compl. para 60 nor the counties can verify), VRA 52 U.S.C. 10307(a), and the Civil Rights Act materiality/different-standards provision 52 U.S.C. 10101(a)(2)(A) (procedure applied only to listed voters; A-number matching cannot reach U.S.-born citizens); (5) no irreparable harm the emergency is "solely due to its own neglect" (roll in hand May 8, Weber notified Jul 16, suit Oct 15); (6) equities: "the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiff's process is credible"; (7) Purcell bars relief; (8) the public interest favors voting rights and election staff. Disposition: "DENIES the Application" (p.26). The order appoints no special master and sets no hearing date, no PI schedule and no ruling on the motions to dismiss. DOJ files a notice of appeal of ECF 149 the same day (ECF 152). A CBS headline the same day read "Court dismisses DOJ's request" (the order is a TRO denial; the case stays open).
rows.s: Order Denying Temporary Restraining Order [62], United States v. California, C.D. Cal. rows.e: Hearing on Los Angeles County Registrar Dean C. Logan's motion to dismiss DOJ's complaint in United States v. California (ECF 68, filed Oct 21) is set for Oct 30, 2026, at 8:30 AM before Judge Carter (per the ECF 68 docket text). rows.e: Scheduled EO 13848 sec. 1(a) DNI assessment of foreign interference in the Nov 3 election, due "Not later than 45 days after the conclusion of" the election (~Dec 18, 2026); the AG/DHS sec. 1(b) report is due "Within 45 days of receiving" it (about Feb 1, 2027), after which Treasury is to "impose all appropriate sanctions" (sec. 3(a)). Precedent: the 2020 1(b) report was finished Feb 2021 and its key findings released Mar 16, 2021; the 2022 report was finished Feb 2023 and released Dec 2023.
rows.w: The designated pre-Jan 3 channel is the DNI 1(a) assessment (due after most state certifications and before the House convenes Jan 3); an early 1(a) or 1(b) is possible. A post-election foreign-interference finding could feed certification challenges (I). The EO has no ballot or machine custody provision of its own, but its 1(b) inputs (2020 and 2022 practice) include FBI forensic analyses: the finding and the evidence come from the same DNI, AG/FBI and DHS leadership (I).

rows.e: Pending, not law: if H.R. 8312 (passed House Jun 10, 2026) is enacted, PRAC's sunset moves from Sept 30, 2034 to Dec 31, 2028, when PRAC "assets" incl. "data use agreements and memoranda of understanding... data, records" transfer to the new Treasury Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery, with the PRAC chair as acting IG "notwithstanding" the Vacancies Act; the new IG is treated as "conducting civil or criminal law enforcement activity for the purposes of section 552a(b)(7)" and is exempt from AG initial determination (5 U.S.C. 406(f)(2)); the DATA Act analysis center changes from "may" to "shall"; $10M authorized only from FY2035; OMB sec. 4 guidance within 270 days of enactment and an OMB directive by Mar 1, 2029. Secs. 2 and 4 (Fiscal Service data program; MOUs and data to agencies for "criminal and other investigations") would take effect on enactment. Covered funds: pandemic, SBA, UI, IIJA, IRA, PACT, CHIPS, P.L. 119-21 programs and federal awards of $50K or more.
